name: Hand and wrist bones (right)
description: Right hand and wrist skeleton: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges, with the distal radius and ulna for context.

source.conversion_notes: Binary STL converted to GLB: vertices welded, smooth normals, axes converted to Y-up/Z-anterior, recentred on the hand, one node per structure. Geometry otherwise unchanged.
source.anatomy_verified: Geometry and identity taken unchanged from BodyParts3D (FMA IDs preserved).

groups.label: Carpal bones
groups.tip: Carpal mnemonic: "So Long To Pinky, Here Comes The Thumb" - Scaphoid, Lunate, Triquetrum, Pisiform (proximal row, thumb to pinky), then Hamate, Capitate, Trapezoid, Trapezium (distal row, pinky to thumb).

groups.label: Metacarpals
groups.tip: Metacarpals are numbered I to V starting at the thumb. Their heads form your knuckles.

groups.label: Phalanges
groups.tip: Each finger has three phalanges (proximal, middle, distal). The thumb has two: 14 in total.

content.origin: Latin radius, "spoke of a wheel" or "ray". The radius turns around the ulna like a spoke.
content.location: The lateral (thumb-side) bone of the forearm. Its wide lower end forms most of the wrist joint.
content.description: A long bone that is narrow at the elbow and broad at the wrist.
content.function: Carries most of the load from the hand to the forearm and rotates around the ulna to turn the palm up and down (supination and pronation).
content.mnemonic: Radius sits by the thumb: "thumbs up for the radius".
content.clinical: A Colles fracture is a break of the distal radius, usually from a fall on an outstretched hand.
content.hint: The big forearm bone on the thumb side, meeting the scaphoid and lunate.

questions.text: Which movement depends on the radius rotating around the ulna?
options: Turning the palm up and down
questions.explanation: The radius rotates around the ulna during pronation and supination.

content.origin: Latin ulna, "elbow" or "forearm".
content.location: The medial (little-finger side) bone of the forearm.
content.description: A long bone that is large at the elbow and small at the wrist, ending in the ulnar styloid process.
content.function: Forms the main hinge of the elbow and acts as the fixed bone the radius rotates around. At the wrist it is separated from the carpal bones by a cartilage disc.
content.mnemonic: Ulna is by the little finger: "U and the little finger point the same way".
content.clinical: The ulnar styloid is often broken together with a distal radius fracture.
content.hint: The forearm bone on the little-finger side.

questions.text: At the wrist, the ulna is separated from the carpal bones by what?
options: Nothing - it joins the lunate directly
questions.explanation: An articular disc (part of the triangular fibrocartilage complex) sits between the ulna and the carpal bones.

content.origin: Greek skaphe, "boat", plus -oeides, "like". It is shaped a little like a boat.
content.location: Proximal row of the carpal bones, on the thumb (lateral) side, next to the radius.
content.description: The largest bone of the proximal carpal row. It is long and curved and bridges the two carpal rows.
content.function: Links the proximal and distal carpal rows, helping the wrist move smoothly and stay stable. It also carries force from the thumb side of the hand to the radius.
content.mnemonic: "Scaphoid sails beside the thumb" - a little boat on the thumb side.
content.clinical: The most commonly fractured carpal bone, usually from a fall on an outstretched hand. Tenderness in the anatomical snuffbox is a warning sign. Its blood supply enters at the far end, so the near part can lose its blood supply after a fracture.
content.hint: Look in the first row of wrist bones, on the thumb side, right next to the radius.

questions.text: Which is the most commonly fractured carpal bone?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone, usually after a fall on an outstretched hand.

questions.text: What is an important role of the scaphoid?
options: It links the two rows of carpal bones
It is a sesamoid bone in a tendon
It forms the knuckle of the index finger
questions.explanation: The scaphoid bridges the proximal and distal carpal rows, helping wrist movement and stability.

content.origin: Latin luna, "moon". Seen from the side it has a crescent-moon shape.
content.location: Centre of the proximal carpal row, between the scaphoid and the triquetrum.
content.description: A crescent-shaped bone that sits in the middle of the wrist, directly beyond the radius.
content.function: Forms part of the main wrist joint with the radius and passes force from the capitate to the forearm.
content.mnemonic: "Lunate is the moon in the middle of the wrist."
content.clinical: The most commonly dislocated carpal bone. Loss of its blood supply causes Kienbock disease.
content.hint: The middle bone of the first row of wrist bones.

questions.text: Which carpal bone is most commonly dislocated?
questions.explanation: The lunate is the most commonly dislocated carpal bone.

questions.text: Where is the lunate?
options: Middle of the proximal carpal row
Little-finger side of the distal row
Inside a tendon on the palm
questions.explanation: The lunate sits in the centre of the proximal row, between the scaphoid and triquetrum.

synonyms: Cuneiform bone of the hand (older term)

content.origin: Latin triquetrus, "three-cornered". It is roughly pyramid-shaped.
content.location: Proximal carpal row on the little-finger (medial) side, beside the lunate. The pisiform sits on its palm side.
content.description: A pyramid-shaped bone with a small oval facet on its front for the pisiform.
content.function: Helps form the ulnar side of the wrist and moves with the other proximal row bones. It transfers load through the cartilage disc to the ulna.
content.mnemonic: "Tri = three corners, on the pinky side."
content.clinical: The second most commonly fractured carpal bone, often as a small chip off its back surface.
content.hint: First row of wrist bones, on the little-finger side, with the pea-shaped pisiform sitting on it.

questions.text: Which bone sits on the palm side of the triquetrum?
questions.explanation: The pisiform articulates with the front (palmar) surface of the triquetrum.

content.origin: Latin pisum, "pea", plus forma, "shape". It is small and pea-shaped.
content.location: On the palm side of the triquetrum, at the little-finger side of the wrist crease.
content.description: The smallest carpal bone. It sits inside the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris.
content.function: Acts as a sesamoid bone, giving the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon better leverage. It is also an attachment point for the flexor retinaculum.
content.mnemonic: "Pisiform is the pea you can feel at the pinky side of the wrist."
content.clinical: It forms one wall of Guyon canal, through which the ulnar nerve and artery pass into the hand.
content.hint: The tiny pea-shaped bone on the palm side of the little-finger edge of the wrist.

questions.text: Why is the pisiform called a sesamoid bone?
options: It is the largest carpal bone
questions.explanation: The pisiform develops within the tendon of flexor carpi ulnaris, which makes it a sesamoid bone.

content.origin: Greek trapezion, "little table", a four-sided figure.
content.location: Distal carpal row on the thumb side, at the base of the first metacarpal.
content.description: An irregular bone with a saddle-shaped surface for the thumb and a groove for the flexor carpi radialis tendon.
content.function: Forms the saddle joint at the base of the thumb, which allows the thumb to move across the palm (opposition).
content.mnemonic: "TrapeziUM sits under the thUMb."
content.clinical: The thumb base joint (trapezium and first metacarpal) is a very common site of osteoarthritis.
content.hint: Second row of wrist bones, directly below the thumb metacarpal.

questions.text: Which movement is made possible by the saddle joint between the trapezium and the first metacarpal?
questions.explanation: The saddle-shaped trapezium lets the thumb move across the palm to touch the other fingers.

questions.text: How can you tell the trapezium from the trapezoid?
options: The trapezium is under the thumb
The trapezium is under the little finger
The trapezium is in the proximal row
The trapezium is inside a tendon
questions.explanation: Remember "trapeziUM under the thUMb". The trapezoid sits next to it, under the index finger.

content.origin: Greek trapezoeides, "table-shaped".
content.location: Distal carpal row, between the trapezium and the capitate, at the base of the second metacarpal.
content.description: A small wedge-shaped bone, the smallest bone of the distal row.
content.function: Holds the base of the index finger metacarpal firmly in place, making the index finger a stable pillar of the hand.
content.mnemonic: "TrapezOID is the Other one - beside the trapezium, under the index finger."
content.clinical: Rarely injured on its own because it is well protected and tightly bound to its neighbours.
content.hint: Second row of wrist bones, between the thumb-side bone and the big central bone.

questions.text: Which metacarpal does the trapezoid mainly support?
questions.explanation: The trapezoid sits at the base of the second (index finger) metacarpal.

content.origin: Latin caput, "head". It has a rounded head that fits into the proximal row.
content.location: Centre of the distal carpal row, at the base of the third metacarpal.
content.description: The largest carpal bone, with a rounded head that sits in a hollow formed by the scaphoid and lunate.
content.function: Acts as the keystone of the wrist. It carries force from the middle finger to the lunate and radius and is the centre of wrist movement.
content.mnemonic: "Capitate is the Captain - biggest and in the centre."
content.clinical: It is the first carpal bone to ossify, which makes it useful when estimating bone age on X-ray.
content.hint: The biggest wrist bone, in the middle of the second row, below the middle finger.

questions.text: Which is the largest carpal bone?
questions.explanation: The capitate is the largest carpal bone and sits in the centre of the distal row.

content.origin: Latin hamus, "hook". It has a hook-like projection on its palm side.
content.location: Distal carpal row on the little-finger side, at the base of the fourth and fifth metacarpals.
content.description: A wedge-shaped bone with a hook (the hook of hamate) that projects towards the palm.
content.function: Supports the ring and little finger metacarpals. Its hook anchors the flexor retinaculum, which forms the roof of the carpal tunnel.
content.mnemonic: "Hamate has a hook - hang your ring and pinky on it."
content.clinical: The hook can break in golf, tennis and baseball when the handle presses into the palm. It is also a boundary of Guyon canal (ulnar nerve).
content.hint: Second row of wrist bones, on the little-finger side. Look for the hook.

questions.text: Which feature gives the hamate its name?
questions.explanation: Hamate comes from the Latin hamus, "hook", after the hook of hamate.

questions.text: In which sport is a fracture of the hook of hamate typically seen?
questions.explanation: A club, racquet or bat handle pressing into the palm can fracture the hook of hamate.

content.origin: Greek meta, "beyond", plus karpos, "wrist": the bones beyond the wrist.
content.location: In the palm, between the carpal bones and the thumb. Metacarpals are numbered from the thumb (I) to the little finger (V).
content.description: A long bone with a base (near the wrist), a shaft and a head (the knuckle). The shortest and thickest metacarpal. It sits at an angle to the others so the thumb can oppose.
content.function: Lets the thumb move independently and powerfully, especially in gripping and pinching.
content.mnemonic: Count from the thumb: thumb = I, so the thumb = I. The heads are your knuckles.
content.clinical: A Bennett fracture is a break into the joint at the base of the first metacarpal.
content.hint: In the palm, in line with the thumb.

questions.text: Which metacarpal is shortest and thickest?
questions.explanation: The first (thumb) metacarpal is the shortest and thickest.

content.origin: Greek meta, "beyond", plus karpos, "wrist": the bones beyond the wrist.
content.location: In the palm, between the carpal bones and the index finger. Metacarpals are numbered from the thumb (I) to the little finger (V).
content.description: A long bone with a base (near the wrist), a shaft and a head (the knuckle). Usually the longest metacarpal, with a notched base that locks against the trapezoid.
content.function: Forms a stable, fixed pillar for the index finger, which is important for precision grip.
content.mnemonic: Count from the thumb: thumb = I, so the index finger = II. The heads are your knuckles.
content.clinical: Because it is firmly fixed at the base, force is often transmitted along it to the carpal bones.
content.hint: In the palm, in line with the index finger.

questions.text: Which carpal bone does the second metacarpal articulate with?
questions.explanation: The second metacarpal articulates with the trapezoid.

content.origin: Greek meta, "beyond", plus karpos, "wrist": the bones beyond the wrist.
content.location: In the palm, between the carpal bones and the middle finger. Metacarpals are numbered from the thumb (I) to the little finger (V).
content.description: A long bone with a base (near the wrist), a shaft and a head (the knuckle). Has a small styloid process at the back of its base.
content.function: Forms the central, most stable pillar of the hand, in line with the capitate.
content.mnemonic: Count from the thumb: thumb = I, so the middle finger = III. The heads are your knuckles.
content.clinical: The styloid process at its base can form an extra bony lump (carpal boss) on the back of the hand.
content.hint: In the palm, in line with the middle finger.

questions.text: Which carpal bone does the third metacarpal articulate with?
questions.explanation: The third metacarpal articulates with the capitate.

content.origin: Greek meta, "beyond", plus karpos, "wrist": the bones beyond the wrist.
content.location: In the palm, between the carpal bones and the ring finger. Metacarpals are numbered from the thumb (I) to the little finger (V).
content.description: A long bone with a base (near the wrist), a shaft and a head (the knuckle). Thinner than the second and third metacarpals and more mobile at its base.
content.function: Supports the ring finger and allows a little movement that helps cup the palm.
content.mnemonic: Count from the thumb: thumb = I, so the ring finger = IV. The heads are your knuckles.
content.clinical: Its neck may break together with the fifth in a punch injury.
content.hint: In the palm, in line with the ring finger.

questions.text: Which carpal bone does the fourth metacarpal articulate with?
questions.explanation: The fourth metacarpal articulates with the hamate (and also the capitate).

content.origin: Greek meta, "beyond", plus karpos, "wrist": the bones beyond the wrist.
content.location: In the palm, between the carpal bones and the little finger. Metacarpals are numbered from the thumb (I) to the little finger (V).
content.description: A long bone with a base (near the wrist), a shaft and a head (the knuckle). The most mobile metacarpal at its base, where it meets the hamate.
content.function: Supports the little finger and lets the ulnar side of the palm cup around objects for a firm grip.
content.mnemonic: Count from the thumb: thumb = I, so the little finger = V. The heads are your knuckles.
content.clinical: A boxer fracture is a break of the neck of the fifth metacarpal, often from punching a hard surface.
content.hint: In the palm, in line with the little finger.

questions.text: A "boxer fracture" most commonly involves which bone?
questions.explanation: A boxer fracture is a break of the neck of the fifth metacarpal.

content.origin: Greek phalanx, "a line of soldiers": the finger bones line up in rows.
content.location: The first bone of the thumb, just beyond the knuckle (metacarpal head).
content.description: The longest phalanx of each digit, with a concave base that fits the rounded metacarpal head.
content.function: Forms the knuckle joint with the metacarpal, which allows the finger to bend, straighten and spread.
content.mnemonic: Proximal = closest to the palm.
content.clinical: Fractures of the proximal phalanx can twist the finger (rotational deformity) if not aligned correctly.
content.hint: The thumb bone closest to the palm.

questions.text: How many phalanges does the thumb have?
questions.explanation: The thumb has only a proximal and a distal phalanx. The other fingers have three.

content.origin: Greek phalanx, "a line of soldiers": the finger bones line up in rows.
content.location: The first bone of the index finger, just beyond the knuckle (metacarpal head).
content.description: The longest phalanx of each digit, with a concave base that fits the rounded metacarpal head.
content.function: Forms the knuckle joint with the metacarpal, which allows the finger to bend, straighten and spread.
content.mnemonic: Proximal = closest to the palm.
content.clinical: Fractures of the proximal phalanx can twist the finger (rotational deformity) if not aligned correctly.
content.hint: The index finger bone closest to the palm.

content.origin: Greek phalanx, "a line of soldiers": the finger bones line up in rows.
content.location: The first bone of the middle finger, just beyond the knuckle (metacarpal head).
content.description: The longest phalanx of each digit, with a concave base that fits the rounded metacarpal head.
content.function: Forms the knuckle joint with the metacarpal, which allows the finger to bend, straighten and spread.
content.mnemonic: Proximal = closest to the palm.
content.clinical: Fractures of the proximal phalanx can twist the finger (rotational deformity) if not aligned correctly.
content.hint: The middle finger bone closest to the palm.

content.origin: Greek phalanx, "a line of soldiers": the finger bones line up in rows.
content.location: The first bone of the ring finger, just beyond the knuckle (metacarpal head).
content.description: The longest phalanx of each digit, with a concave base that fits the rounded metacarpal head.
content.function: Forms the knuckle joint with the metacarpal, which allows the finger to bend, straighten and spread.
content.mnemonic: Proximal = closest to the palm.
content.clinical: Fractures of the proximal phalanx can twist the finger (rotational deformity) if not aligned correctly.
content.hint: The ring finger bone closest to the palm.

content.origin: Greek phalanx, "a line of soldiers": the finger bones line up in rows.
content.location: The first bone of the little finger, just beyond the knuckle (metacarpal head).
content.description: The longest phalanx of each digit, with a concave base that fits the rounded metacarpal head.
content.function: Forms the knuckle joint with the metacarpal, which allows the finger to bend, straighten and spread.
content.mnemonic: Proximal = closest to the palm.
content.clinical: Fractures of the proximal phalanx can twist the finger (rotational deformity) if not aligned correctly.
content.hint: The little finger bone closest to the palm.

content.origin: Greek phalanx, "a line of soldiers": the finger bones line up in rows.
content.location: The middle bone of the index finger. The thumb has no middle phalanx.
content.description: Shorter than the proximal phalanx, with joints at both ends.
content.function: Adds a second bending joint to the finger. The flexor digitorum superficialis tendon attaches here to bend the middle finger joint.
content.mnemonic: Middle = in the middle, and the thumb skips it.
content.clinical: Injury to the middle finger joint can cause a boutonniere or swan-neck deformity.
content.hint: The middle bone of the index finger.

content.origin: Greek phalanx, "a line of soldiers": the finger bones line up in rows.
content.location: The middle bone of the middle finger. The thumb has no middle phalanx.
content.description: Shorter than the proximal phalanx, with joints at both ends.
content.function: Adds a second bending joint to the finger. The flexor digitorum superficialis tendon attaches here to bend the middle finger joint.
content.mnemonic: Middle = in the middle, and the thumb skips it.
content.clinical: Injury to the middle finger joint can cause a boutonniere or swan-neck deformity.
content.hint: The middle bone of the middle finger.

questions.text: Which digit has no middle phalanx?
questions.explanation: The thumb has only proximal and distal phalanges.

content.origin: Greek phalanx, "a line of soldiers": the finger bones line up in rows.
content.location: The middle bone of the ring finger. The thumb has no middle phalanx.
content.description: Shorter than the proximal phalanx, with joints at both ends.
content.function: Adds a second bending joint to the finger. The flexor digitorum superficialis tendon attaches here to bend the middle finger joint.
content.mnemonic: Middle = in the middle, and the thumb skips it.
content.clinical: Injury to the middle finger joint can cause a boutonniere or swan-neck deformity.
content.hint: The middle bone of the ring finger.

content.location: The middle bone of the little finger. The thumb has no middle phalanx.
content.description: Shorter than the proximal phalanx, with joints at both ends.
content.function: Adds a second bending joint to the finger. The flexor digitorum superficialis tendon attaches here to bend the middle finger joint.
content.mnemonic: Middle = in the middle, and the thumb skips it.
content.clinical: Injury to the middle finger joint can cause a boutonniere or swan-neck deformity.
content.hint: The middle bone of the little finger.

content.origin: Greek phalanx, "a line of soldiers": the finger bones line up in rows.
content.location: The fingertip bone of the thumb.
content.description: A small bone with a rough, flattened tip (the tuberosity) that supports the fingertip pulp and nail.
content.function: Supports the fingertip and nail for fine touch and pinch. The deep flexor tendon attaches here to bend the fingertip.
content.mnemonic: Distal = distant from the palm: the fingertip.
content.clinical: Crush injuries often break the tip (tuft fracture). Mallet finger is an injury to the extensor tendon at the base of this bone.
content.hint: The tip bone of the thumb.

content.origin: Greek phalanx, "a line of soldiers": the finger bones line up in rows.
content.location: The fingertip bone of the index finger.
content.description: A small bone with a rough, flattened tip (the tuberosity) that supports the fingertip pulp and nail.
content.function: Supports the fingertip and nail for fine touch and pinch. The deep flexor tendon attaches here to bend the fingertip.
content.mnemonic: Distal = distant from the palm: the fingertip.
content.clinical: Crush injuries often break the tip (tuft fracture). Mallet finger is an injury to the extensor tendon at the base of this bone.
content.hint: The tip bone of the index finger.

questions.text: What is "mallet finger"?
options: A tendon injury at the distal phalanx so the fingertip droops
A break of the fifth metacarpal
questions.explanation: Mallet finger is an injury to the extensor tendon where it attaches to the distal phalanx, so the fingertip cannot straighten.
